title: SA/33/2015 of Nem Chandra Vs Smt Gayatri Devi AND ANOTHER

paras.text:
IN THE HIGH COURT OF UTTARAKHAND AT NAINITAL
SECOND APPEAL NO. 33/2015
Nem Chandra
 ÖÖÖ Appellant
Versus
Smt. Gayatri Devi & Another
 ÖÖÖ. Respondents
Mr. Siddhartha Sah, Advocate, for the appellant/defendant no. 1.
Mr. Jitendra Chaudhary, Advocate, for the caveator/respondent no.
1/plaintiff.
Mr. S.S. Chauhan, Advocate, for the proforma respondent/defendant no. 2.
3rd March, 2015

Honíble Servesh Kumar Gupta, J.
Having heard learned Counsel for the parties, it
transpires that a registered sale deed of the property, in
dispute, was executed on 5.7.1994 by Ahmad Noor in
favour of plaintiff Smt. Gayatri Devi. It appears that she
was living over the property in question even before such
execution of sale deed.
Just five days prior to such sale deed, a
notarised agreement to sell was got executed by the
appellant Nem Chandra from Mr. Ramesh, the husband of
Smt. Gayatri Devi. It appears that he was also living within
the premises of the same property since before such
notarised deed.
An Original Suit No. 167/95 was launched by
Smt. Gayatri Devi seeking eviction of Nem Chandra as well
as for the quashing of entries of the municipal assessment,
which had got done by Nem Chandra on the basis of that
agreement to sell.
Nem Chandra contested the suit and filed the
written statement on 3.12.1996. The suit was finally
decreed on 23.11.2011, whereagainst an appeal was
preferred by Nem Chandra and that too was dismissed on
merits on 2.12.2014. So, this second appeal has been

2
preferred challenging the validity of the judgments passed
by both the Courts below.
The contention of learned Counsel for the
appellant is that both the reliefs should not have been
granted by the regular Civil Court and, as per Section 16 of
the Provincial Small Cause Courts Act, the matter should
have been instituted in the Small Causes Court. Learned
Counsel of the appellant also argued that as per Article 4 of
the Second Schedule of the said Act, the suit was not
maintainable before the regular Civil Court. He further
argued that the entries of municipal assessment should
have been challenged, under the U.P. Municipal Act, before
the District Collector, and not in the Civil Court.
I feel that this second appeal has no force
because after instituting the suit on 22.7.1995, Mr. Nem
Chandra filed the written statement almost after one and
half years and then protracted the civil litigation for almost
15 years in the trial court. Section 23 of the Provincial
Small Cause Courts Act specifically makes the provision
that where the question of proof of title over the immovable
property is concerned, the regular Civil Court, and not the
Judge, Small Causes Court, is the proper forum to
determine the issue. As is apparent, the second appellant
Nem Chandra did not have any title over the property, in
question, because no immovable property could be
transferred merely on the basis of a notarised agreement to
sell. Further, there was no occasion for the husband of
Smt. Gayatri Devi to make such an agreement in favour of
Nem Chandra.
In the given facts and circumstances, it is
obvious that the status of Nem Chandra was nothing but of
an illegal occupant in the said premises.
So far as the prayer for quashing the entries of
the municipal assessment is concerned, the same is a

3
consequential relief which naturally arises on account of
the grant of the first relief.
For the reasons recorded above, I find no force in
this second appeal. It is dismissed at the very threshold.
